script.opening: “Hello, doctor. I’ve had a couple of choking episodes, and the one last week really frightened the life out of us. Normally I’d ask my MND nurse, but she’s off sick, so here I am.”

facts.text: “Twice in three weeks. Last Wednesday, rice — it went down the wrong way, I couldn’t breathe for a few seconds. Sunita hit me on the back and it came up.” No blue lips, no collapse. Since then he eats soft food and takes small mouthfuls.
“Water makes me cough most. Thick things are easier. My tablets are a struggle — I crush the riluzole.” Food sometimes sticks. Saliva: “more spit than I can manage — I keep a hanky.”
“Meals take forever. I’ve lost weight — I was 74 kilos in the summer, 69 this morning.” You can show the bathroom scale reading on your phone if asked.

facts.topic: Breathing and sleep (only if asked about breathing, sleep or headaches)
facts.text: “Now you mention it, I wake with a headache most mornings, and I nod off in the afternoon. I can’t lie flat any more — I sleep on three pillows or I get puffed.” Not breathless sitting. No cough with phlegm, no fever.
“Sunita says I’m slurring a bit by evening.” (On video, his speech is slightly nasal and slurred.)
Two falls in two months, tripping on the right foot. No head injury. Walks with a stick, slowly. Arms “still OK”.

facts.topic: Mood and fears (if asked how he is coping or what worries him)
facts.text: “I’m a pharmacist — I’ve read everything. I know where this goes.” If the doctor gently asks what he fears most: “Choking to death. Drowning in my own spit.” Then, if invited further: “And I don’t want to be kept alive on a machine if it comes to that. I haven’t said that to Sunita.”
Lives with wife Sunita, 62, a dentist, at work until 6 pm. Son in Manchester. Bungalow. Financially secure. Never smoked, no alcohol.

Be calm, articulate and slightly clinical about yourself — a professional who has done his reading. Reveal the breathing and sleep symptoms only if asked about breathing, sleep or headaches. Reveal the fear of choking and wishes about machines only if the doctor asks what worries you or what matters to you, and gives you space. If rushed, keep it to yourself. You cannot attend today (no one to drive you); a home visit tomorrow evening or Sunita bringing you would work.

ice.ideas: “My MND is reaching my swallowing — I knew it would.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terrified of choking to death, and wants to talk about not being kept alive on machines, which he has not yet discussed with his wife.
ice.expectations: Practical help with the choking now his nurse is away, and someone to talk to about what comes next.

cues: “Frightened the life out of us.” — fear behind a calm manner.
“I’m a pharmacist — I know where this goes.” — he has thought about the future.
“I can’t lie flat any more.” — respiratory muscle weakness.

checkpoints.text: Assesses the choking and swallowing: frequency, consistency (thin liquids worse), saliva, tablets, aspiration signs (cough, fever, chest infection)
Asks about weight loss, speech, mobility and falls, and specifically about respiratory weakness — orthopnoea, morning headaches, daytime sleepiness, disturbed sleep
Explores his understanding, mood and fears, discovering the fear of choking to death and his wishes about life-prolonging treatment
Arranges urgent speech and language therapy and dietitian input, and urgent MND team/neurology or respiratory contact for NIV assessment and a gastrostomy discussion
Addresses medicines and symptoms: liquid riluzole via the specialist or pharmacist rather than crushing; saliva management; OT and physiotherapy for falls; home visit when his wife is present

Gives safe-swallow and choking first-aid advice (including for Sunita), safety-nets for aspiration and breathlessness, and offers to begin advance care planning (wishes, ADRT, ReSPECT, LPA) at his pace
Responds to fear with honest reassurance (death from choking is rare in MND), respects his expertise, and supports him to involve his wife

worked.txt: “Can I ask about your breathing at night — do you wake with headaches, feel sleepy in the day, or find it hard to lie flat?”
“You’ve read a lot. When you think ahead, what worries you most?”
“Many people with MND fear choking to death. It’s actually rare — most people die peacefully, often in their sleep, and there are medicines and plans that help if breathing or choking becomes hard.”
“It sounds like you have clear views about machines and tubes. Would it help to start writing down what matters to you — and to talk it through with Sunita, with me there if you like?”

f.learning: In established MND the GP’s role is to recognise progression early and mobilise the multidisciplinary team quickly — especially when the specialist nurse is unavailable. Bulbar weakness causes dysphagia, coughing with thin fluids, sialorrhoea and weight loss; respiratory muscle weakness causes orthopnoea, morning headaches, daytime sleepiness and poor sleep, and should prompt urgent respiratory assessment for non-invasive ventilation, which can improve survival and quality of life. NICE advises discussing gastrostomy early and placing it before significant respiratory decline and weight loss; weight loss of 5% or more is a trigger for action. Riluzole is available as an oral suspension for people who cannot swallow tablets. Advance care planning should be offered at diagnosis and at each significant change: preferences, advance decision to refuse treatment (for example about NIV or feeding), ReSPECT, lasting power of attorney for health and welfare, preferred place of care, and anticipatory medicines. Reassure honestly: death from choking in MND is uncommon.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG42 Motor neurone disease: assessment and management (2016, updated 2019) · Mental Capacity Act 2005 (advance decisions and lasting power of attorney) · Resuscitation Council UK ReSPECT process (version 3, 2020) · NICE NG31 Care of dying adults in the last days of life (2015) · MND Association guidance for GPs (accessed 2026)
knowledge.summary: Progressing bulbar and respiratory weakness with 7% weight loss: urgent SALT, dietitian, NIV and gastrostomy discussions via the MND team, safer medicines, falls support — and an advance care planning conversation guided by his fears.

points.t: Coughing with thin fluids, prolonged meals, food sticking, drooling and weight loss suggest bulbar progression. Speech and language therapy assesses safe consistencies and strategies (upright posture, small mouthfuls, chin tuck, thickened fluids). Dietitian for calorie and fluid intake.

Discuss early, before swallowing becomes unsafe or weight loss is marked (5% or more is a trigger), and ideally while respiratory function allows safe placement. It can supplement rather than replace oral intake.

Orthopnoea, morning headaches, daytime sleepiness, unrefreshing sleep, poor cough and recurrent infections. Needs urgent assessment (FVC/SNIP, blood gases) and consideration of non-invasive ventilation. Previous FVC 78% does not exclude current decline.

Thin saliva: options include hyoscine patches, glycopyrronium, amitriptyline or atropine drops (specialist advice). Thick secretions: hydration, humidification. Riluzole oral suspension is available; ask the specialist team or pharmacist before crushing tablets.
Teach carers back blows and abdominal thrusts; 999 if obstruction persists. A cough-assist device may be considered by respiratory services. Death from choking is uncommon in MND.

Explore values and wishes; ADRT for specific treatments (must be written, signed and witnessed, stating “even if life is at risk” for life-sustaining treatment); ReSPECT; LPA for health and welfare; preferred place of care and death; anticipatory (“just in case”) medicines; Gold Standards Framework or palliative care register.

model.text: Hello Mr Mehta, it’s Dr Owusu. Can you see and hear me? I’m sorry your nurse is away — tell me about the choking.
model.why: Acknowledges the gap in his usual care

model.text: Twice in three weeks. Last week rice went down the wrong way — Sunita had to hit my back. It frightened us both.
That sounds really frightening. Is it solids, liquids, or both? Any coughing after drinks, trouble with tablets or saliva, chest infections or fevers?
Water’s the worst. I crush my riluzole. Lots of saliva. No fevers.
Has your weight changed? And can I ask about your breathing at night — headaches in the morning, sleepiness in the day, or trouble lying flat?
74 to 69 kilos. Actually yes — morning headaches, nodding off, three pillows or I get puffed.
Thank you, that’s important. Any falls, and how is your speech?
Two falls, no head injury. Sunita says I slur by evening.
You know this illness well. When you think ahead, what worries you most?
model.why: Opens space for the hidden agenda

model.text: Choking to death. And I don’t want to be kept alive on a machine. I haven’t told Sunita that.

Thank you for telling me. Many people fear choking, but dying from it is rare in MND — and there are treatments and plans that help. Your wishes about machines matter, and we can write them down so they’re respected.

Things have moved on: your swallowing, weight and the night-time breathing. I’ll make urgent referrals today to speech and language therapy and a dietitian, and contact the neurology team about a breathing assessment — a mask at night can help — and a talk about a feeding tube, which you can decide about. I’ll ask about riluzole as a liquid and something for the saliva, and get the falls team out.
model.why: Urgent MDT referrals and symptom control

model.text: I’d want to think carefully about the tube and the mask.
Of course — it’s your decision, and knowing the options early keeps them open. Could I visit tomorrow evening when Sunita is home? We could talk through what matters to you together, at your pace.

Until then: sit upright, small mouthfuls, slow down, thicker drinks are easier. If you choke and it doesn’t clear, Sunita should call 999. Fever, a chesty cough or worse breathlessness — call us or 111. What will you tell Sunita tonight?
model.why: Safe-swallow, choking and aspiration safety-net; teach-back

model.text: That you’re coming tomorrow, about the referrals — and that I want to talk about what I want if things get worse.

social.t: His knowledge is an asset; respecting it builds partnership, but he still needs space for fear.
Sunita works full-time; carer’s assessment, choking first aid, and her own support matter.

legal.t: An ADRT refusing life-sustaining treatment must be written, signed, witnessed and state that it applies even if life is at risk. An LPA for health and welfare must be registered with the Office of the Public Guardian.

professional.t: When a key specialist is unavailable, the GP must escalate through the team rather than wait for the nurse to return.

community.t: MND Association (support visitors, equipment loans, grants); specialist palliative care; community OT and physiotherapy; speech and language therapy; dietitian.

psychosocial: Who is at home and when
ice: Expectation: practical help and someone to talk to

playbook.diagnosis: Progression of ALS with bulbar dysphagia, aspiration risk, sialorrhoea, 7% weight loss, probable nocturnal hypoventilation and falls.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The MND is now affecting the muscles for swallowing and, at night, breathing. There’s a lot we can do to make both safer.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re frightened of choking, and you know what you would and wouldn’t want. Let’s make things safer now and make sure your wishes are known.”
management.psychosocial: Home visit with Sunita; carer support; MND Association.
sharedPlan: Urgent MND team/neurology or respiratory contact: NIV assessment and gastrostomy discussion
Advance care planning at his pace: wishes, ADRT, ReSPECT, LPA
safetyNet: Fever, chesty cough or worse breathing — GP or 111 same day

pitfalls.intro: Candidates often give swallow advice and a SALT referral, missing the night-time breathing and the conversation he wants to have.

items.fail: Never asks about sleep, headaches or lying flat.
items.why: Respiratory muscle weakness is the major threat to life and is treatable with NIV.
items.fix: Ask about orthopnoea, morning headaches and daytime sleepiness at every MND review.

items.fail: Refers to SALT and waits for the MND nurse to return.
items.why: Weight loss and hypoventilation need urgent action now.
items.fix: Escalate via the neurology team or respiratory services today.

items.fail: Raises DNACPR abruptly as a checklist item.
items.why: Advance care planning should follow his concerns and pace.
items.fix: Ask what worries him and what matters to him first.

wordPics.clearFail: Advises soft food and a routine SALT referral; no weight, respiratory or emotional assessment.
wordPics.fail: Arranges SALT and dietitian but misses the respiratory symptoms, or attempts DNACPR without exploring his wishes.
wordPics.pass: Assesses swallow, weight and night-time breathing, makes urgent MDT referrals (SALT, dietitian, NIV, gastrostomy discussion), addresses riluzole and falls, safety-nets and opens advance care planning.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, plus: draws out his fear of choking and wishes about machines, reassures honestly, respects his expertise and autonomy, and arranges a joint conversation with Sunita at his pace.
